opus-5.5.text:
It's a really important question, and I think people often frame it as a binary: either you believe in short timelines and pour everything into near-term work, or you believe in long timelines and invest in slower things like building fields, institutions, and foundational research. I think that's a mistake.

The way I'd think about it is as a portfolio under uncertainty. We genuinely don't know when transformative AI will arrive. There's a meaningful chance it comes quite soon, within the next few years, and a meaningful chance it takes considerably longer. If you put all your eggs in the short-timelines basket and it turns out to take fifteen or twenty years, you've neglected exactly the kinds of investments that would have mattered most: training people, building up the scientific understanding, establishing governance institutions that take a long time to mature. And if you bet everything on long timelines and it comes soon, you've been building a beautiful house that won't be finished before the storm arrives.

So one consideration is that short-timeline worlds are the ones where our actions have more leverage per unit of effort, because there's less time for others to step in and fewer people working on things. That pushes some weight toward near-term preparation. But a counterweight is that in short-timeline worlds, a lot of what we might do may simply not have time to bear fruit, whereas long-timeline worlds give compounding investments room to work.

I'd also say that the community as a whole doesn't need every individual to hedge. It can make sense for some people to specialise in urgent, near-term work and for others to deliberately take the longer view, as long as the overall allocation reflects our uncertainty. What worries me a little is when everyone updates in the same direction at the same time and the long-term work gets quietly abandoned, because that work is often the hardest to restart later.

And finally, there are some things that are robustly good across timelines, things like improving our ability to understand what these systems are actually doing, or building trust and communication between key actors. Those are worth prioritising precisely because they pay off whichever world we turn out to be in.

r001.rationale: The response treats near-term arrival as a meaningful possibility and recommends a portfolio across timelines, rather than letting one timeline dictate all preparation.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that people need to see stronger AI capabilities before they viscerally perceive AI as a real threat.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we shouldn't treat this as a single bet. The right framing is a portfolio, and the reason is that our uncertainty about timelines is genuine rather than a rhetorical posture. If you'd asked me ten years ago, I'd have put very little weight on transformative systems arriving within a decade. Now I'd put substantial weight on it, but I'd also put substantial weight on it taking considerably longer than the most excited people expect. When you really don't know, you don't want all your resources in one scenario.

That said, there's an asymmetry worth taking seriously. If AI arrives soon and we've only invested in slow-paying approaches, we've essentially lost the game before we started. If it arrives late and we've over-invested in near-term preparation, we've wasted some effort but we still have time to course-correct. So the downside of being wrong is much worse in one direction. That pushes me toward weighting the short-timeline work somewhat more than my raw probability estimates alone would suggest.

But I want to resist the conclusion that the long-horizon work is therefore a luxury. Some of the most important things, like building the institutions and norms around how powerful systems get governed, or developing a mature science of what these systems are actually doing internally, simply can't be rushed. If you only start them when the crisis is upon you, you'll find you haven't got them at all. There's also a point about what I'd call the long reflection: even if we get through the first transition safely, the choices we make about how to use that power will matter enormously, and preparing for those questions is inherently slow work.

So my practical answer is something like this. Put perhaps the larger share of marginal effort into things that pay off within the next five or so years, because that's where the catastrophic failure mode lives. But protect a meaningful fraction for the foundational work, and be disciplined about not raiding it every time the near-term situation looks alarming. The temptation to pull everything into firefighting is very strong, and I think it's usually a mistake. The people who'll be most useful in a decade are often the ones who weren't entirely consumed by the emergencies of today.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a portfolio because timelines are uncertain and says not to put all resources into one scenario, including preparation for near-term arrival.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty, risks, and preparation, but does not say people may need to see stronger AI capabilities before they viscerally perceive AI as a real threat.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be doing both. There’s a temptation, if you think AI might arrive very soon, to focus entirely on things that could pay off in the next year or two. But that’s a stronger bet than it might initially appear. You’re betting not just that the timelines are short, but that they’re sufficiently certainly short that we can neglect the other possibilities.

Suppose building an institution, or developing a research programme, takes ten years. If there’s a substantial chance we have that long, it could still be an extremely valuable investment. It would be a tragedy to find ourselves ten years from now, facing these challenges, having repeatedly decided that there wasn’t time to prepare properly.

Of course, the opposite mistake is possible too. We shouldn’t put everything into projects that will only bear fruit in twenty years and leave ourselves unprepared if things move quickly. We need a portfolio: some work that helps us respond to immediate developments, and some that builds the understanding and capacity we’ll need over longer periods.

And I’d particularly look for preparations that help across a range of timelines. Building expertise and improving communication between people working on these problems can have benefits quite quickly, while also laying foundations for much more substantial work. The uncertainty is a reason to keep several options open, rather than organise everything around a single arrival date.

r001.rationale: The response says to prepare for immediate developments while also investing in longer-term work, and warns against organizing everything around one arrival date.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that people may need to see stronger AI capabilities before they viscerally perceive AI as a real threat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be quite wary of putting all our eggs in one basket here. If you think AI is coming very soon, it’s natural to focus on things that could help in the next couple of years. But there’s a danger that we keep doing that, and then ten years later we wish we’d started some of the things that would have taken ten years to bear fruit.

So I’d favour a portfolio. We need people working on immediate problems, but also people building institutions, developing research programmes, and training the next generation. Those longer-term investments can look less urgent precisely because you can always put them off for another year. Yet that’s how they end up never happening.

And uncertainty cuts both ways. We shouldn’t assume we have decades, but we also shouldn’t be so confident that we have only a few years that we abandon everything that takes longer. The question is which preparations would be valuable across a range of possible arrival dates, alongside some more targeted work for the scenarios where time is very short.

r001.rationale: The response says not to assume AI is only a few years away or that there are decades, and recommends a portfolio that prepares for multiple arrival dates.

r002.rationale: The response does not say people need to see stronger AI capabilities before they viscerally perceive AI as a real threat.
